summary.text: The Roman Senate was the highest and constituting assembly of ancient Rome and its aristocracy, lasting from the Roman Kingdom into the Middle Ages.
Under the kings it was little more than an advisory council, though it also elected new kings.
It reached the apex of its republican power by the middle Republic, then declined from the late Republic and lost much of its political power under the Principate.

The people's assembly, with no say from elders
The Senate, whose pick the people then formally elected
The army's generals, by acclaim

Plebeians outnumbered patricians among senators

items.prompt: Latin senex means 'old man'. What does the word senatus therefore mean?

options.label: A council of generals
A house of city founders
A gathering of all free citizens
An assembly of elders

items.explain: The word senatus derives from senex, so it means assembly of elders.

items.prompt: How do historians relate the Roman Senate to bodies like modern parliaments?

options.label: As an exact copy with the same powers
As a distant predecessor, though its powers varied widely
As unrelated, since it was only a ceremonial club
As the creator of every constitution in Europe

items.explain: The Senate can be considered a distant ancestor of parliamentarism and modern legislatures, although its functions and powers varied considerably.

items.prompt: In the Republic, which body regulated incoming and outgoing treasury transactions and handed out grants for public buildings?

options.label: The Senate, passing grants on to the Censors
The Censors, who paid for everything themselves
The consuls, from their own private wealth
The people's assembly, by popular vote

items.explain: The Senate held fiscal responsibility for the treasury and alone could distribute grants to the Censors for public buildings.

The constitutional reforms of Diocletian

paragraphs.heading: An assembly of elders
paragraphs.text: The Roman Senate was the highest assembly of ancient Rome and of its aristocracy. Its Latin name, senatus, comes from senex, meaning 'old man', so the word means an assembly of elders; English borrowed it as senate. It lasted from Rome's first days, through the Kingdom, the Republic and the Empire, and on as the Byzantine Senate into the Middle Ages, with powers that kept changing along the way.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: Its roots lay in the gens, or clan: a group of families under a living male head called a pater, Latin for father. As the early clans came together into one community, the patres of the leading clans were chosen for a shared council of elders that grew into the senate. Tradition says Rome's first king, Romulus, created it with 100 men, whose descendants became the patrician class. The fifth king added another 100, and in 509 BC Rome's first and third consuls, Brutus and Publicola, brought new men in and raised it to 300.

paragraphs.heading: Under the kings
paragraphs.text: While Rome had kings, the senate was mostly an advisory council. Its biggest job was picking each new king: the people formally voted, but it was the senate that really chose him and approved him both before and after the vote. A king could ignore the senate's advice, yet its growing prestige made that harder and harder to do. Only the king could make new laws, though he often brought both the senate and the people's assembly into the process.

paragraphs.heading: In the early Republic
paragraphs.text: When the Republic began in 509 BC, the senate had 300 to 500 members who sat for life. At first only patricians belonged; plebeians were let in later. Early on it was weak next to the magistrates, the officials who appointed senators. Because the shift from monarchy to constitutional rule was probably gradual, it took several generations for the senate to gain the upper hand. It oversaw money flowing in and out of the treasury, and it was in charge of public buildings, since only it could hand out grants to the censors.

paragraphs.heading: Peak and decline
paragraphs.text: By the middle Republic the senate stood at the height of its power. Its decline began in the late Republic, after the reforms of the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus. When the Republic gave way to the Principate, it lost much of its power and its prestige. After Emperor Diocletian's reforms it no longer mattered politically, and once government moved away from Rome it shrank to a purely local city body. Constantine the Great's creation of a second senate in Constantinople lowered its standing further.

paragraphs.heading: A long afterlife
paragraphs.text: After Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476, the western senate carried on under Odoacer and then under Ostrogothic rule. Justinian I's reconquest of Italy restored its official status, but it vanished after 603, the year of its last recorded public act. The eastern senate in Constantinople lasted into the early 13th century. Some medieval Roman nobles held the title senator, but only as an honour. In name and in role, the Roman Senate can be seen as a distant ancestor of parliaments and modern legislatures.
